newsitem.title: CHINA: New HK leader may be heading for constitutional row.
newsitem.headline: New HK leader may be heading for constitutional row.

text.p: Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa may be headed for a constitutional crisis after pushing emotive laws to deport illegal children and suspend labour laws in his first two weeks in office, lawyers said on Sunday.
The measures have set off a storm of protests in Hong Kong, which was handed over to communist China on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule.
"It is highly symbolic that at the very first of its public sittings the provisional legislature showed its true colour and real role," said Margaret Ng, a former pro-democracy legislator.
Ng and other pro-democracy lawmakers refused to join the new Beijing-appointed legislature, charging it illegally replaced a colonial assembly elected to a four-year term in 1995.
Tung brought howls from civil liberties activists by quickly submitting laws to deport illegal immigrants, curb labour union rights and set out voting reforms before elections in 1998.
The children immigration law, the first passed by the new legislature, amended Hong Kong's Basic Law, a mini-constitution that went into force at the handover from British rule.
"The precedent is set that rights given by the Basic Law can be taken away by the provisional legislature," Ng said. "The next thing is to see whether the judiciary will concur."

Scores of lawyers have volunteered to help defend as many as 2,000 children who have poured into Hong Kong illegally over the past year, believing the Basic Law gave them the right of abode because one of their parents was a Hong Kong resident.

The legislature amended the Basic Law, and made the move retroactive to July 1. The children must now have proper papers before arriving from mainland China and can be deported if they are in Hong Kong illegally.
"I think people see that the issues involved have very far-reaching and constitutional implications," Bar Association president Audrey Eu told reporters.
Tung, a former shipping magnate who was China's choice for chief executive, has sought to play down the legal challenges and questions about whether the legislature has overstepped its powers.
"Hong Kong is a very free society. People can take the government to court on all these issues," he said on Saturday after returning from a quick trip to Beijing.
Tung's government is also being challenged over its proposal to suspend three labour laws, which were passed in the twilight of British rule and give labour unions more powers.
One trade union leader is on a hunger strike. Pro-democracy advocates and trade unionists plan to join forces on Sunday for a march through central Hong Kong.
Even pro-China legislators, such as Tsang Yok Sing who voted against the labour laws in the colonial assembly, have expressed reservations about suspending the laws now.
"Now they have been duly passed and are consistent with the Basic Law. Any attempt to repeal or amend them should proceed very carefully," he said.
A shadow was cast over the legislature even before it held its first regular session, with a number of challenges to its legitimacy as a body. One test case is headed to the Court of Final Appeal.

Tsang said he, like other lawmakers, was confident that the courts would reject the challenges to the legitimacy of the new legislature but that if the body were found to be illegal, it would spark a constitutional crisis.

"The government would have to deal with a period of three to four months without a legislature and that is a constitutional crisis. I think the courts will take that into consideration," he told Reuters.
